title: Crossair 498

title: Kenya Airways 431
summary: Kenya Airways Flight 431 crashed into the Atlantic Ocean shortly after takeoff from Abidjan on 30 January 2000 at night. The crew responded to a false stall warning by pushing the control column forward, placing the aircraft into an unintended descent. The GPWS warnings were masked by priority stall and overspeed warnings in conditions with no external visual references. The Commission of Inquiry concluded the pilot applied stall recovery procedure while the airplane was not in a true stall situation.

The pilot flying's action on the control column put the airplane into a descent without the crew realizing it. The GPWS warnings were masked by priority stall and overspeed warnings. The conditions for takeoff towards the sea at night provided no external visual references.

summary: Alaska Airlines Flight 261, a McDonnell Douglas MD-83 flying from Puerto Vallarta toward Seattle with a stop in San Francisco, suffered a catastrophic loss of pitch control on 31 January 2000 after the horizontal stabilizer trim system's jackscrew assembly failed from worn acme nut threads, and crashed into the Pacific Ocean near Anacapa Island, California, while diverting to Los Angeles. The crew struggled for over two hours with a jammed stabilizer, and when they finally freed it using the primary trim system, it moved to an extreme nose-down position, forcing the aircraft into a nosedive from about 31,050 ft. The NTSB attributed the crash to inadequate maintenance that allowed excessive jackscrew wear, killing all 88 aboard.

title: Vologda Aviation Enterprise 9651
summary: Vologda Aviation Enterprise Flight 9651, a Yakovlev Yak-40D, began takeoff from Moscow Sheremetyevo Airport at 8:42 a.m. on March 9, 2000. At approximately 49 feet above ground, the aircraft entered a stall accompanied by an uncontrollable bank to the left. The investigation found the pilots failed to set the required flap configuration for takeoff (flaps set to 11 degrees instead of required 20 degrees) and did not adequately deice the aircraft, with excess ice on wings combined with engine surging from incorrect configuration preventing sufficient lift.

title: 2000 Charles de Gaulle runway collision
summary: At Paris–Charles de Gaulle Airport on May 25, 2000, the night tower controller made a critical mental model error, believing that Streamline Aviation Flight 200 (Shorts 330, registration G-SSWN) was positioned behind Air Liberté Flight 8807 (McDonnell Douglas MD-83, registration F-GHED) when it was actually on the runway entering from taxiway 16. Flight 8807 was cleared for takeoff and began its roll. Flight 200 attempted to brake after making visual contact via beacon lights but was unable to avoid impact. The MD-83's left wing struck the Shorts' cockpit at approximately 155 knots during the takeoff roll. The first officer of Flight 200 was killed instantly; the captain sustained serious injuries. title: Hapag-Lloyd 3378

title: Gulf Air 072
summary: Gulf Air Flight 072, an Airbus A320-212 flying from Cairo to Bahrain, crashed into the shallow waters of the Persian Gulf 2 km from the airport on 23 August 2000, minutes after a go-around from a failed approach to Runway 12. The captain suffered spatial disorientation, applying a large nose-down input that produced a 15-degree dive; as the aircraft descended, the crew disregarded the GPWS 'sink rate' and 'Whoop, whoop, pull up' warnings while debating flap configuration instead. The Airbus struck the sea at 280 knots, killing all 143 people on board.
probable_cause: The final report found non-adherence to Standard Operating Procedures and loss of spatial and situational awareness by the crew during the approach and go-around, compounded by deficient CRM training at Gulf Air and safety oversight failures by the civil aviation authority.

factors.evidence: The flight crew suffered from spatial disorientation during the go-around and crashed into the shallow waters of the Persian Gulf.
Non-adherence to a number of Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) by the aircraft crew during the approach and final phases of the flight.
Systemic factors also contributed to the accident, including deficiency in crew resource management (CRM) training by Gulf Air.
Instead of responding to the sink rate warning, the captain ordered flap retraction as the GPWS escalated to 'Whoop, whoop! Pull up!'
Safety oversights by the Directorate General Of Civil Aviation and Meteorology of Oman.
Flying with a speed of 280 knots and a nose-down pitch of 6.5 degrees, the aircraft slammed onto the sea below, instantly killing all 143 passengers and crew members.

events.text: Captain Shakeeb applied a large nose-down input, inducing a rapid descent at a pitch angle of approximately 15 degrees, the maximum permissible, as the aircraft continued to accelerate under TO/GA thrust.
As the first officer called 'flaps three,' the Ground Proximity Warning System issued a 'sink rate' alert, but instead of responding to the warning, the captain ordered flap retraction.
As the aircraft descended toward the sea, the GPWS escalated to 'Whoop, whoop! Pull up!' while the crew continued discussing flap position as the aircraft descended unchecked.
At 19:30, flying at 280 knots with a nose-down pitch of 6.5 degrees, the aircraft slammed onto the sea, instantly killing all 143 passengers and crew members.

notes: Investigating agency not explicitly named in the trimmed article text; only 'the final report' and the Omani civil aviation directorate are mentioned.

title: 2000 Australia Beechcraft King Air crash
summary: A chartered Beechcraft climbed to 34,300 feet above its cleared altitude of 25,000 feet. The pilot and passengers became incapacitated from hypoxia because the aircraft lacked a high cabin altitude aural warning device and supplemental oxygen was not used. The autopilot maintained level flight on a north-easterly heading for five hours as the left engine exhausted fuel. The aircraft crashed 65 km southeast of Burketown with all eight occupants killed.
probable_cause: The incapacitation of the pilot and passengers was probably due to hypobaric hypoxia because of the high cabin altitude and their not receiving supplemental oxygen. The reasons for the pilot and passengers not receiving supplemental oxygen could not be determined.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was not fitted with a high cabin altitude aural warning device, nor was it required to be.
The incapacitation of the pilot and passengers was probably due to hypobaric hypoxia because of the high cabin altitude.
After the aircraft climbed above the assigned altitude of FL250, the speech and breathing patterns of the pilot displayed changes consistent with hypoxia.
The ATSB found it likely that the autopilot was engaged, and this caused the aircraft to fly on a straight heading.
Towards the end of the flight, the left engine stopped due to fuel exhaustion.
The aircraft continued flying on a straight north-easterly heading for five hours, before exhausting its fuel and crashing 65 km south-east of Burketown.

events.text: Aircraft departed Perth at 18:09 local time (10:09 UTC) with seven mine workers and crew aboard.
Aircraft cleared to climb to FL250 and instructed to be at FL160 by 36 nmi from Perth.
At FL256, pilot replied Sierra Kilo Charlie standby when ATC asked to confirm altitude; aircraft continued climbing above assigned level.
ATC attempted regain contact with pilot, controller called Sierra Kilo Charlie Melbourne Centre, if receiving this transmission squawk ident.
Aircraft left radar coverage at FL343 (34,300 feet) passing 32,500 feet altitude.
Business jet reported aircraft in level flight at FL343 with no visible movement of flight controls.
Left engine stopped due to fuel exhaustion; aircraft descended and crashed into ground 65 km southeast of Burketown.

title: Aeroméxico 250
summary: The DC-9-31 overran the runway on landing at General Lucio Blanco International Airport in Reynosa during adverse weather caused by the remains of Hurricane Keith. The aircraft landed late on the runway at 4:55 pm local time when storm conditions and heavy rain were present. The airplane landed nearly halfway down the 1,900-meter runway and could not stop before the runway end. After overrunning the runway, the aircraft struck trees and crashed into houses of the Francisco Sarabia neighborhood, breaking into three pieces. All 88 people on board survived, but 64 were injured; four ground residents were killed.
probable_cause: The pilots landed late on the runway due to errors in the approach procedure during adverse weather conditions caused by Hurricane Keith remnants. The runway was inundated by heavy rains, which annulled the braking system effects.

The pilots landed late on the runway due to errors in the approach procedure that became inaccurate.
After overrunning the runway the plane hit trees and crashed into houses.
The aircraft broke in three pieces but did not catch fire.

title: Singapore Airlines 006
summary: During heavy rain from Typhoon Xangsane with poor visibility, the aircraft was cleared for takeoff but lined up on the closed runway 05R instead of the assigned runway 05L. The pilots did not see construction equipment on the closed runway and collided with excavators and other machinery after 41 seconds at full throttle. The aircraft broke apart and caught fire, destroying the forward fuselage section. The accident exposed systemic failures including the lack of ground radar, absence of physical barriers or hazard markings on the closed runway, and active taxiway lighting that guided pilots into the construction zone.
probable_cause: The flight crew lined up on the wrong runway due to poor visibility and turned 215 meters too soon. However, the investigation found that ATC cleared takeoff without operational ground radar and the airport lacked proper physical barriers and hazard markings on the closed runway.

The airport was not at the time equipped with ASDE, which is a ground radar that enables air traffic controllers to detect potential runway conflicts
The runway contained concrete Jersey barriers and pits, but there were no physical barriers or hazard markings on the closed runway
About 41 seconds after applying full throttle, the aircraft collided with construction machinery including excavators, vibrating rollers, a bulldozer, and an air compressor parked on runway 05R
A large fire destroyed the forward section of the fuselage and the wings

title: 2000 ASA Pesada Antonov An-24 crash
summary: On 15 November 2000, an Antonov An-24 operated by ASA Pesada crashed shortly after taking off from Quatro de Fevereiro Airport in Luanda, Angola, banking left before hitting a field in the Golfe II district and exploding; all 57 aboard were killed. title: Dirgantara Air Service 3130
summary: The Britten-Norman Islander, carrying 18 people including the captain and 17 passengers, took off from Datah Dawai. The aircraft was overloaded and rotated at 70 knots instead of the recommended 55-60 knots. Shortly after takeoff, the aircraft failed to gain adequate altitude due to overloading, struck trees in the forest, and crashed upside down. All 18 occupants were injured but none were killed.
probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Committee concluded the crash was caused by multiple factors: pilot error from incorrect perception about takeoff speeds, aircraft overloading caused by bribery, and lack of safety infrastructure at the airport.

factors.evidence: The aircraft was overloaded, as proven by the fact it only reached 150 ft altitude at a range of 6000 ft when it should have gained 200 ft.
Captain Abdul rotated at 70 knots, faster than the aircraft's recommended takeoff speed of 55-60 knots.
The captain held an incorrect mental model that taking off at higher speed would improve obstacle clearance, when in fact it reduced available climb performance.
The captain attempted an unpublished turn-back maneuver by veering left to avoid trees, rather than following established procedures.
The aircraft continued to lose altitude with sharp nose-down pitch and could not recover.
The aircraft struck trees and crashed into the forest near the airport.

events.text: Captain Abdul rotated at 70 knots and the Britten-Norman Islander took off from Datah Dawai with 17 passengers and 2 infants on board.

The aircraft struck the first tree and started veering to the left.
The aircraft struck the second tree and began zigzagging.
The aircraft struck the third tree and started to lose control.
The landing gear struck the last tree and the aircraft crashed upside down into the forest floor, both wings ripped off from the fuselage.

title: Sabena 877
summary: Sabena Flight 877 was fired upon by Hutu rebels during approach to land at Bujumbura Airport on 4 December 2000. Machine gun fire at 330 feet lasted 20 seconds and damaged nose wheel hydraulics. All 170 people survived with two injuries. Investigation concluded rebels mistakenly believed aircraft was carrying weapons related to a peace agreement.

title: British Airways 2069
summary: At cruise level 42,000 feet, a mentally unstable Kenyan passenger stormed the flight deck and attempted to seize control of the Boeing 747. The passenger attacked the first officer and grabbed the yoke, causing the aircraft to climb sharply and stall from 42,000 feet with a descent rate of 30,000 feet per minute. Captain Hagan emerged from rest break to assist, and with help from two passengers and two flight attendants, successfully removed the assailant. First Officer Watson recovered the aircraft to level flight. Minor injuries occurred from violent pitch changes; the aircraft continued to Nairobi. The captain and crew were later honored for their actions.
